Use a single flat unit namespace: `units/<owner>--<subject>--<contract>/`. The directory identifies only the unit; it conveys no class, layer, domain, lifecycle, or status. A unit is separate when any one of its public contract, accountable owner/release promise, rights boundary, provenance/regeneration mechanism, or execution/failure contract differs. Each unit has a committed `unit.json` manifest and a normal `package.json` where executable/package metadata is needed. output.design:
Adopt a flat workspace namespace: `units/<unit-id>/package.json`, with no category-bearing parent directories. `unit-id` is a stable kebab-case product noun, not a type label; package names are `@oaknational/<unit-id>`. A directory establishes only the unit boundary. Source files sit at the unit root or use non-classifying module paths; tests are co-located as `*.test.ts`.

A unit is separate when it has a different externally observable contract, delivery/support promise, provenance or refresh authority, assurance/failure boundary, or independently deployable/publishable runtime. It is not separate merely because it is large, has many symbols, or uses a different framework. Split adapters from reusable mechanisms when their consumers or failure modes differ.

Each `package.json` has an `oakUnit` object. The minimal independent classifications are: `interface` (how consumers interact: `import`, `invoke`, `serve`, or `material`); `delivery` (the support/distribution promise: `public-package`, `deployed-product`, `internal`, `demonstration`, `research`, or `operations`); `provenance` (the authority over contents: `authored`, `curated`, `third-party-pinned`, `external-feed`, or `generated-ephemeral`); and `assurance` (a set of risk profiles such as `standard`, `security-critical`, `production`, `evidence`, `live-operation`, and `hook`). A fifth value, `graphLayer`, is derived rather than authored from the workspace dependency graph.

Example: `{ "oakUnit": { "interface":"import", "delivery":"public-package", "provenance":"authored", "assurance":["standard"], "graphLayer":"derived" } }`.

`graphLayer` is recomputed on every validation run from declared runtime imports: leaf primitives must not depend on higher layers; adapters depend inward; deployable/invoked units are graph sinks. The graph is evidence, not a substitute for the four declared classifications.

Generated output is written only to a content-addressed artifact store or deployment staging area. Its producing unit keeps reproducible source, generation declaration, input digests, and artifact coordinates in version control—never the regenerated bytes. Consumers declare an artifact dependency by producer ID and digest/compatibility range; build orchestration materialises it outside Git. External feeds use the same mechanism, but their manifests also record provider, schema/format contract, refresh owner, trigger, and retention/licence terms.

Enforcement: JSON-schema validation requires every workspace manifest to carry `oakUnit`; a workspace validator rejects category-bearing workspace paths, duplicate unit IDs, undeclared cross-unit imports, generated files tracked by Git, and imports that violate the derived graph direction. Dependency-cruiser/ESLint resolves imports against manifest contracts. Turbo task policies are generated from `delivery`, `provenance`, and `assurance`: production/evidence units enter their required gates; operational units require explicit runbooks and live-operation checks but are not silently treated as product-tested; hook adapters run their fast hook-safe checks. Publish/deploy configuration is checked against `delivery`; licence and integrity checks are checked against `provenance`.

This makes the current distinction visible without preserving it as path taxonomy: the live manifests show deployable applications, demos, libraries, a public curriculum SDK, code-generation work, design assets/system, graph libraries, and agent tooling, while Turbo already distinguishes generated outputs and build consumers. The proposal moves those meanings to explicit declarations rather than `apps/`, `packages/core/`, `packages/libs/`, `packages/sdks/`, `demos/`, or `research/` paths.

Use a shallow workspace of independently coherent packages, with only two internal levels: `packages/<domain>/<unit>/`. A unit is a package when it has its own public contract, change/validation lifecycle, ownership boundary, distribution terms, or dependency-policy role. Do not create packages merely for folders, tiny helpers, or hypothetical reuse; those stay as modules within their owning unit until they acquire one of those boundaries. Every package has a guessed, stable noun-based path and a machine-readable `unit.json`; generated material always lives beneath the unit that owns its publication or consumption contract, never in a generic catch-all.

Top-level layout: `packages/foundation/*` (small cross-estate primitives), `packages/platform/*` (generic integrations and machinery), `packages/domain/<domain>/*` (product-specific capabilities), `packages/apps/*` (deployed or demonstrator applications), `packages/operations/*` (live-system operations), `packages/evidence/*` (non-shipping studies), `packages/content/*` (licensed reference data and protected assets), and `packages/tooling/*` (developer tooling). Each package exposes only declared entry points; implementation uses `src/`, tests use `test/`, and owned outputs use `generated/<producer-or-event>/`. A host that serves another unit's built output declares it as an explicit build input rather than owning or copying its source.

`unit.json` is the one manifest for the organisation: identity, owner(s), source authority, generation policy, consumers, release channel, distribution/licence, validation commands, and allowed dependency classes. The workspace package manifest remains the package-manager carrier. Dependency direction is computed from package imports and checked as a graph. The package path is the first lookup route; a root-generated machine index is only an accelerator, not a second taxonomy. Splitting preserves the old facade temporarily and moves one contract/lifecycle at a time; merging moves contracts into one unit, removes the edge, and retires only the obsolete facade. Thus scale adds sibling units rather than new roots, while a bad classification normally changes one manifest, one package path, and graph policy—not the whole estate.

output.design:
Contract-first leaf workspaces with orthogonal policy metadata.

Questions answered
1. What is an independently governable unit?
2. Which differences require a boundary, and which merely require internal modules?
3. Where does each kind of unit live?
4. How is a unit named without confusing technology, provider, audience, and domain?
5. Who owns it, who consumes it, and what support promise does it carry?
6. What may it depend on, and what may depend on it?
7. How are generated, externally fetched, curated, vendored, and authored material kept distinct?
8. How are incompatible rights, runtimes, privileges, and quality regimes separated?
9. Who owns cross-unit built artefacts?
10. How are boundaries enforced and later reconsidered?

Unit definition
A unit is a leaf workspace directory with one package.json, one human owner, one coherent externally visible responsibility, explicit entry points or artefacts, and one value for every governing classification. Code, tests, and fixtures may remain together only while their rights, origin, execution boundary, service promise, and assurance regime agree. There are no nested units. Data and asset units are also registered workspaces, normally private, so they participate in the same dependency and ownership graph.

Untracked, disposable build output is not a unit. A generated output becomes a unit when it is tracked, published, embedded elsewhere, refreshed independently, or consumed by more than its producer.

Mandatory split rule
Split when either side has a different licence class; origin or edit policy; regeneration trigger or update mechanism; independently consumed or delivered output; runtime privilege or credential envelope; audience/support promise; quality regime; human custody; or semantic scope that would otherwise conceal a prohibited dependency. Different consumers or failure modes also require separate executable entry-point units even when their change rhythm is identical. A shared pure library may sit beneath them when real common behaviour exists.

Keep material together when all classifications agree, it is always released and supported as one contract, it has no independent consumers or owner, and separation would add an edge without creating an enforceable boundary. File count, public-symbol count, similar directory structure, and change frequency alone neither split nor merge a unit.

The minimal independent classifications are: mechanical kind, semantic area, portability, service promise, execution/trust boundary, origin/lifecycle, rights, assurance profile, and human ownership. None can be inferred safely from another: for example, evidence code can use product gates without being shipped, and a product and demo can share structure while carrying different promises. Dependency role is deliberately derived from the graph rather than declared as a tenth classification.

Manifest contract
Every leaf has standard name, type, private, license, exports, scripts, and dependencies fields plus an estate object containing kind, area, portability, service, execution, origin, gateProfile, assuranceFlags, owner, produces, consumes, and any expiring waiver. Origin is a tagged value: authored; curated; generated with producer and trigger; external-snapshot with upstream, mechanism, and trigger; or vendored-byte-preserved with source and checksum. Credential references identify capabilities only; secrets never appear in manifests.

apps/demo/{<demo-one>,<demo-two>}
packages/foundation/error

packages/design/{system,tokens,interactive-widget}
packages/adapters/{search-cluster-retrieval,observability-provider,auth-provider}
tools/libraries/<capability>
tools/commands/<capability>
tools/guards/<capability>
tools/validators/<capability>
tools/jobs/<capability>
tools/generators/<capability>

datasets/snapshots/<source-contract>
datasets/bulk/<dataset>

Directories carry coarse form; manifests carry orthogonal policy. Libraries use @estate/<area>-<capability>. Other forms use @estate/<form>-<area>-<capability>. The scope is a placeholder for the real publishing organisation. Names describe the contract, not its generator, refresh rate, or current implementation. Vague leaves such as common, shared, utils, or core are rejected unless paired with a concrete capability.

Dependency and enforcement model
A validator constructs one graph from package dependencies, TypeScript imports, declared artefact edges, and build tasks. Cross-unit relative imports, deep imports outside exports, undeclared file copying, and inter-unit cycles fail. Universal packages cannot import commodity, domain, product, repository, study, or operations code. Commodity adapters cannot import curriculum or product code. Domain packages cannot import applications, demos, repository tooling, studies, or operations. Applications, demos, studies, operations, and executable tools are sinks. Repository, study, and operations closures are forbidden from entering shipped product closures.

An artefact unit owns its generated files and runs its generation task using declared producer libraries and inputs. Producers do not write directly into consumers. Consumers depend on the artefact unit and copy it only during packaging. Exactly one producer is allowed for every generated artefact.

Changed-unit checks are selected from gateProfile and run over the affected unit plus the appropriate reverse-dependency closure in the turbo graph. Separate checks enforce path/manifest agreement, licence homogeneity, public exports, deterministic generation, snapshot provenance, vendor checksums, immutable generated and vendored paths, human ownership, forbidden graph edges, and deploy-closure purity. Graph fan-in, fan-out, strongly connected components, artefact propagation, and repeated multi-unit changes are review signals; they do not automatically rewrite semantic boundaries.

output.design:
Use one flat address space: `units/<unit-id>/`, with no subgroup directories and no classification encoded by path. `<unit-id>` is a stable identity token only, e.g. `curriculum-client`, not a type or tier. Every unit contains a versioned `unit.json` manifest and flat, role-prefixed files such as `api-*.ts`, `impl-*.ts`, `test-*.ts`, `fixture-*.json`, and `run-*.ts`. The newcomer entry point is always `units/<guessed-id>/unit.json`; the root `estate.json` is the complete index and resolves aliases/search terms to unit IDs.

The independent classifications are deliberately limited to: responsibility contract, custody/provenance, execution-and-assurance profile, and outward-terms. Dependency permissions, change impact, regeneration edges, consumers, and release eligibility are derived relations, not another taxonomy. A unit is separate when it has a separately changeable public contract, custody/provenance, execution profile, or outward terms. Otherwise it remains part of its existing unit. Split by extracting one such boundary and redirecting callers through a declared API; merge by retiring one ID, migrating its contract edges, and retaining an alias/tombstone for one release window.

`unit.json` declares `id`, `aliases`, `purpose`, `publicApi`, `owners`, `custody`, `execution`, `assurance`, `terms`, `inputs`, `outputs`, `allowedDependencies`, and `replacementFor`/`replacedBy` where applicable. `estate.json` indexes those manifests, validates uniqueness, and materializes a dependency-and-impact graph. No generated artefact is tracked: rebuild outputs go to a content-addressed external build store or deployment artifact store, with source manifests recording only the generator, input digest, and published artifact digest.

Imports are permitted only from a dependency's declared `publicApi`, only when the source manifest explicitly lists that dependency, and only where the dependency's terms and execution constraints permit it. A graph checker rejects undeclared, internal, cyclic, forbidden-profile, and forbidden-terms imports; TypeScript project references and package export maps make the intended boundary practical; commit-time guards run the fast subset and CI runs the complete graph, provenance, licence, and regeneration checks. The impact command walks reverse dependency, regeneration, deployment, and owner edges and reports required follow-up units plus the checks that will run. Scaling doubles rows in the root index and graph, not path depth; machines read the index then one manifest before opening implementation files.

Decide placement with this rule: code lives with the narrowest stable owner that can change it without forcing unrelated consumers to change, provided its dependencies point inward, its licence is uniform, and its source/generation authority is explicit. organisingRules.name: C1 Consumption form

organisingRules.name: C2 Capability identity
organisingRules.rule: A unit owns one independently explainable capability. Names are stable, kebab-case and domain-first, such as curriculum-client or repo-state-validator. Ban shared, common, utils and misc. Use visible role suffixes such as -demo, -hook, -job, -study, -live-ops, -snapshot, -bundle and -adapter where they prevent operational mistakes.
organisingRules.carrier: The directory slug equals the @estate/<slug> package-name suffix; estateUnit.capability supplies the machine-readable identity. Package exports define its usable contract.

organisingRules.name: C3 Accountability and byte authority
organisingRules.rule: Every unit has exactly one accountable human owner and one mode determining who may set its bytes: authored, curated, fetched, generated, vendored or built. AI agents may act for an owner but are never the accountable owner. Humans directly edit only authored or curated bytes.
organisingRules.carrier: estateUnit.owner and estateUnit.custody with mode, writer, provenance and replacement command. CI rejects direct edits to fetched, generated, vendored or built trees; vendored material also has byte hashes.

organisingRules.name: C4 Renewal event
organisingRules.rule: Every machine-managed unit has one event class and one replacement mechanism. Different triggers require different units even when provider, credential or command is shared. Observed frequency schedules work but is not identity.
organisingRules.carrier: estateUnit.renewal with event, mechanism, producer, inputs and reproduce command, plus produces or fetches graph edges. Reproduction checks must recreate the complete unit.

organisingRules.name: C5 Rights class
organisingRules.rule: Every unit is legally homogeneous. MIT code, OGL content, reserved brand material and exact third-party rights never occupy the same unit. Fetched and generated derivatives require an explicit resolved rights class rather than inheriting one by assumption.
organisingRules.carrier: The standard license field plus estateUnit.rights containing exact SPDX or LicenseRef value, provenance and required notice. Validation scans file ownership, publication sets and persisted build outputs.

organisingRules.name: C6 Visibility and delivery
organisingRules.rule: Visibility answers who may receive or depend on a unit: public, estate-wide, named consumers or unit-private. Delivery channel is public package, deployed, embedded, workspace-only or non-shipping. A public client must not leak private workspace dependencies.
organisingRules.carrier: Standard private, exports, files, bin and publish configuration plus estateUnit.visibility, estateUnit.delivery and allowedConsumers. Reverse-dependency and publication-closure checks enforce them.

organisingRules.name: C7 Support promise
organisingRules.rule: Production, supported-internal, demonstration, experimental and no-support are distinct promises. Publicness and deployment do not imply production support. Product and demo applications are separate even when structurally identical.
organisingRules.carrier: estateUnit.support, a mandatory -demo suffix for demonstrations, and deployment-root graph checks. Production closures may not contain demonstration or experimental programs.

organisingRules.name: C8 Execution and failure contract
organisingRules.rule: Each program has one primary invoker and failure meaning: end user, maintainer-interactive, commit-blocking, scheduled, build, evidence study or live operation. Programs with different consumers or failure policies are separate; reusable pure logic moves to a library.
organisingRules.carrier: estateUnit.execution with invoker, failurePolicy, target and named capabilities, reinforced by bin and role suffixes. Capability checks ensure credentials reach only approved executable roots.

organisingRules.name: C9 Assurance obligation
organisingRules.rule: Assurance is independent of shipping. Evidence code can use the full product baseline while remaining non-shipping; live operations use a separate operations baseline. Security, reproducibility, byte-integrity and licence controls are additive.
